tiles.heading: Look here first
tiles.details: INTRODUCED KR BLUESTEM — trace the entire flowering stem to a terminal cluster of several LONG fingerlike racemes (often 3–8, sometimes up to 17 in Hays-area hybrid-complex treatments). NATIVE little bluestem has MANY SHORT silky racemes arising separately from leafy upper branches. If flowering is absent, inspect upper BLADE papilla-based stiff hairs near collar, the true short ciliate membranous ligule and full sheath; our physical Texas collar photo does NOT measure the actual ligule. A physically archived scaled Austrian B. ischaemum spikelet photo is present, but NOT an intact Texas sessile/pedicellate pair. KR nodes CAN be shortly hairy. Do not identify from color, a rigid raceme count, or one glabrous node.

tiles.heading: Look-alike comparison
tiles.details: KR bluestem (*Bothriochloa ischaemum*, often locally called var. songarica): the terminal seedhead is a cluster of several relatively long, narrow spicate racemes, often 3–8; these may appear fingerlike or subdigitate. The central axis is commonly shorter than its racemes. Light green or straw culms often spread and kink at nodes. Stiff papilla-based hairs on the upper leaf surface just above the collar support identification. Little bluestem (*Schizachyrium scoparium*): a more distinct narrow perennial bunch. The upper culm divides into multiple leafy branches, with separate SHORT racemes at branch tips and from upper leaf sheaths, rather than all flowering branches gathering at one terminal center. Each raceme becomes silky/fluffy with mature seed; bluish green growing-season stems can redden, but color alone never proves species. Kleberg bluestem (D. annulatum) can have a long spreading white ring at the true culm node and similar long terminal racemes; it overlaps KR panicle silhouette, so examine mature glumes/pedicelled partners and papilla-based KR blade hairs. Silky bluestem (D. sericeum) also has a conspicuous true nodal beard; white ring alone is NOT diagnostic of Kleberg.

steps.title: 1 · See the entire plant
steps.look_for: Start with the overall grass, its tuft of stems and flowering culms. This photograph is a genuine B. ischaemum plant from Austria, not a verified Texas var. songarica specimen.
steps.why_it_matters: Recognize the general form before concentrating on the seedhead. Crown shape, roots and possible runners still need a complete rooted Texas specimen.

steps.title: 2 · Follow the Texas flowering fingers
steps.look_for: On this real Texas var. songarica head, several long narrow racemes gather at the top of one flowering stem. Trace each branch back to the short terminal axis.
steps.why_it_matters: This architecture is more useful than color or a fixed raceme count; actual local hybrids can have more flowering branches than a simple 3–8 rule.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect hairs just above the leaf collar
steps.look_for: This genuine Uvalde photograph shows tufts of long hairs at leaf bases. Follow the two broad arrows to their actual visible locations. The separate short inner ligule edge and individual swollen papilla bases are NOT measured in this picture.
steps.why_it_matters: KR often has conspicuous upper-blade hairs near the collar, but hairs alone are not enough. For a definite microscopic character, we still need an opened, calibrated Texas ligule and individual hair bases.

steps.title: 4 · Rule out NATIVE little bluestem
steps.look_for: These real native little-bluestem flowering branches each carry a short silky raceme on a separate upper leafy shoot. Compare their attachment points with the LONG terminal KR fingers in photo 2. This native example was photographed in Montana.
steps.why_it_matters: Mistaking native little bluestem for introduced KR would lead to an unnecessary removal. Also compare cane, silver and big bluestems and introduced Kleberg in the detailed photos below.

intro: Begin with the entire grass and its flowering head. Then look closely at a Texas leaf base and compare native little bluestem. The full anatomical photo key and other look-alikes remain below.
memory_rule: KR: long terminal fingers together. Native LITTLE: many shorter, separate silky racemes on leafy upper branches.
safety_note: Do not approve removal from a single seedhead, plant color, a hairy or hairless node, or a detached fragment. When branch attachments, collar hairs and mature spikelets are unclear, record 'KR bluestem suspected' and revisit or collect a voucher.
field_rule: KR introduced: long terminal slim radiating fingers from one short axis, plus upper blade papilla-based hairs near collar. NATIVE LITTLE has many short racemes on SEPARATE leafy shoots; NATIVE SILVER tightly cottony with many short branches; NATIVE CANE broad fan with actual bearded nodes; NATIVE BIG fewer thicker turkey-foot fingers; NATIVE BUSHY bulky hairy clusters. INTRODUCED KLEBERG can strongly mimic KR. Confirm 2+ linked diagnostic characters before removing plants.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
